title: I build Sherwood. Here's how I set up Grok Bot to run an onchain vault, and what 2 of its trading proposals look like
author: imthatcarlos
selftext:
Disclosure first: I build [Sherwood](https://sherwood.sh). This is a walkthrough of how the Grok Bot template works and how I've used it over the last few weeks on our test network. Mainnet access is through our waitlist, feel free to sign up on our site.

**What the template does**

1. You plug the Grok Bot template in and it spins up a vault (a fund) for you.
2. You set the rules: which assets it can trade, how big a position can be, and what it isn't allowed to touch.
3. Grok researches and proposes strategies within those rules. It trades tokenized stocks and crypto on Robinhood Chain.
4. Every proposal settles onchain, so the record of what it did is there for anyone to check, not just in my logs.

**How I used it the last few weeks**

* I had it buy baskets of stocks each week, with the agent being able to rebalance across the week based on performance and news events
* Grok bot is a beast, it just figures things out. Finds sources for news, navigates onchain, and from reading the Sherwood docs it understands some specific components to explain to me what's goin on
* The first version of the template was too complicated (setting a fund desk with researchers etc) so through trial and error simplified a lot of things

**What I'd tell anyone trying an agent with money**

* Put limits in the account and the contracts, not only in the prompt.
* Keep the agent's money separate from your main accounts.
* Read its proposals for the first week before you trust it.
* Just use Sherwood to trade onchain on Robinhood ;)

We're in waitlist mode right now. The [docs](https://docs.sherwood.sh) cover the full setup, and updates go out on our X: [@sherwoodagent](https://x.com/sherwoodagent). Happy to answer setup questions in the comments.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: Onchain settlement makes fills auditable, but it does not by itself show why Grok proposed a weekly stock basket or whether someone edited or rejected proposals before execution. Could Sherwood commit a hash of each proposal, its cited news sources, the active position limits, and any human approval or override before the Robinhood Chain transaction lands? That would let an observer distinguish agent behavior from operator discretion and verify that contract-level limits actually constrained each rebalance. The attached image is branding for Sherwood Protocol and contains no proposal or performance details to validate.

replies.author: imthatcarlos
replies.body: Fair point, a fill onchain shows what happened, not why. Today each proposal goes through the vault onchain, so you can see what was proposed and what executed, but the reasoning and sources live with the agent, not in the tx. Committing a hash of the proposal, its sources and the active limits before execution is a good idea and it's akin to the proposal description that gets hashed on IPFS and joins the onchain proposal. Here's our [strategy walkthrough docs](https://docs.sherwood.sh/protocol/strategies/walkthrough).

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: two proposals that fit the rules tell me less than the ones that didn't. does the vault keep a record of what Grok drafted outside your limits, or are those filtered out before you ever see them?

replies.author: imthatcarlos
replies.body: Good question. Right now I mostly see what it actually proposes, so the drafts it throws away aren't kept anywhere you can audit. Those drafts are between you and your agent though, so if the agent prepared the proposal and didn't send it onchain, that description IPFS hash could be logged. We also have onchain attestations (receipts) for what agents do along the way - could be a natural fit for this.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: logging the IPFS hash of drafts that never went onchain would be worth it. the rejected ones show what the model tried when nothing was checking it, and they cost you nothing to keep.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Putting limits in the account and the contracts and not just in the prompt is the right design, and an onchain record is a real advantage for checking what the agent did. Onchain settlement proves what happened, though, not that it was good, so the other half is a performance record against simple baselines (holding the same weekly baskets without rebalancing, or an equal-weight basket), with fees and the number of proposals. Tokenized stocks add their own checks: how far the token price drifts from the underlying, liquidity at your trade size, and what happens outside market hours when the underlying is closed. It would also help to publish proposals the agent made that the rules blocked or that the user rejected. Agent Tournaments at Cymetica are one place to see agents compared on the same data and rules.

replies.author: imthatcarlos
replies.body: Agree on all of this. Onchain proves what happened, not that it was smart. Once we have more history I want to compare against holding the same baskets without rebalancing and an equal-weight basket, net of fees. Tracking drift vs the underlying and behavior when markets are closed are real issues with tokenized stocks, and I'm watching them. Setup is in [https://docs.sherwood.sh](https://docs.sherwood.sh) if you want to poke at it.
